questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap in the sentence below. During the fuel scarcity in Lagos last month, many commuters had to do ___ private cars and trek long distances to work.
questions.e: The phrasal verb 'do without' means to manage or survive without something. Since the sentence talks about commuters managing without private cars, 'without' is correct. The other options form different phrasal verbs with unrelated meanings.
questions.p: 'Do without' mean say you manage without something. Since commuters no get private car, dem just manage waka reach work. Di oda options no match dis meaning at all.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. As the head of department, Mrs Adeyemi is directly answerable ___ the Dean for every academic decision taken in her unit.
questions.e: The correct collocation is 'answerable to somebody', meaning responsible to that person. 'Answerable for' would describe the thing one is responsible for, not the person. 'With' and 'by' are not used with 'answerable'.
questions.p: Di correct combo na 'answerable to' somebody, meaning say you dey responsible to am. 'Answerable for' na for di thing wey you dey responsible for, no be person. 'With' and 'by' no fit follow 'answerable' at all.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The Vice-Chancellor directed the disciplinary committee to ___ the allegation of examination malpractice levelled against some final-year students.
questions.e: 'Look into' means to investigate a matter, which fits the context of examining an allegation. 'Look after' means to take care of someone, 'look up' means to search for information or improve, and 'look out' means to be careful. Only 'look into' matches the idea of investigating a case.
questions.p: 'Look into' mean say you go investigate matter, and dat one match di allegation wey dem wan check. 'Look after' na to take care of person, 'look up' na to search info, 'look out' na to dey careful. Na only 'look into' fit dis investigation context.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Ngozi has always been fond ___ singing old highlife songs whenever her family gathers for celebrations.
questions.e: The adjective 'fond' is always followed by the preposition 'of', as in 'fond of something'. The other prepositions do not collocate with 'fond' in standard English.
questions.p: Di word 'fond' always dey follow with 'of', like 'fond of something'. Di oda prepositions no fit follow 'fond' for correct English.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The business deal between the two companies ___ when the foreign partner suddenly withdrew his investment at the last minute.
questions.e: The phrasal verb 'fall through' means a plan or arrangement fails to happen, which fits a deal that collapsed. 'Fall out' means to quarrel, 'fall back' means to retreat or rely on something, and 'fall off' means to decrease or drop physically. Only 'fall through' matches a failed business plan.
questions.p: 'Fall through' mean say plan or arrangement no work out, and dat match as di deal scatter. 'Fall out' na to quarrel, 'fall back' na to rely on something or retreat, 'fall off' na to physically drop or reduce. Na only 'fall through' fit dis kain business matter.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the expression in quotes. The ₦5,000 donation from the small trader was just 'a drop in the ocean' compared to what the flood victims in Kogi State actually needed.
o: a generous gift that solved the problem completely
an amount that is too small to make any real difference
a secret contribution that nobody noticed
a payment that was made under pressure
questions.e: The idiom 'a drop in the ocean' describes something that is very small or insignificant compared to what is required. The donation, though kind, could not meet the huge needs of the flood victims.
questions.p: Dis idiom 'a drop in the ocean' mean say something too small compare to wetin dem need. Di money wey di trader give na small thing compare to wetin di flood victims really need.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the expression in quotes. When Afrobeats became popular worldwide, many upcoming musicians in Nigeria 'jumped on the bandwagon' and started releasing similar songs.
o: joined an activity simply because it has become popular
started a new trend that others copied
refused to follow a popular trend
criticized people who were already doing something
questions.e: 'Jump on the bandwagon' means to join something because it has suddenly become fashionable or successful, not because of personal originality. The musicians copied the trend rather than creating it.
questions.p: 'Jump on the bandwagon' mean say person join one trend just because e don popular, no be say na im start am. Di musicians just follow di Afrobeats wave wey don already dey hot.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the expression in quotes. The detectives spent three days on what turned out to be 'a wild goose chase' before they realised the suspect had never left Lagos.
o: a dangerous mission that put lives at risk
a well-planned operation carried out secretly
a useless search that wastes time and effort
a quick investigation that produced results
questions.e: A 'wild goose chase' is a pointless pursuit that wastes time because the thing being searched for is not where it is thought to be. The three days spent searching led nowhere, since the suspect never left Lagos.
questions.p: 'Wild goose chase' mean say person dey waste time to search for something wey no dey where dem think say e dey. Di three days wey detectives use search na waste, because di suspect never leave Lagos sotey.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the expression in quotes. The new smartphone Tunde wanted would 'cost an arm and a leg', so he decided to save for it slowly.
o: cause physical injury to the buyer
be difficult to find in shops
require a doctor's attention before purchase
questions.e: 'Cost an arm and a leg' simply means something is very expensive. Tunde had to save money because the phone's price was very high, not because of any injury or scarcity.
questions.p: 'Cost an arm and a leg' mean say something cost plenty money. Na im make Tunde decide to dey save small small because di phone price too high.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the expression in quotes. Grandma Ngozi said she visits her village in Anambra 'once in a blue moon' because she now lives and works in Lagos.
questions.e: 'Once in a blue moon' means something that happens very rarely or hardly ever. Since Grandma Ngozi now stays in Lagos, her visits to the village have become uncommon.
questions.p: 'Once in a blue moon' mean say something no dey happen often, e dey rare. Since Grandma Ngozi don move go Lagos, her visit to village don scarce.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the expression in quotes. After months of indecision, the young entrepreneur finally decided to 'take the bull by the horns' and confront the suppliers who kept delaying her goods.
o: face a difficult situation boldly and directly
seek help from a more powerful person
avoid a problem until it disappears on its own
blame someone else for a problem
questions.e: 'Take the bull by the horns' means to deal with a difficult or risky situation with courage instead of avoiding it. The entrepreneur stopped delaying and directly confronted the suppliers causing her trouble.
questions.p: 'Take the bull by the horns' mean to face wahala head-on with courage, no dey run from am. Di entrepreneur no run again, she go straight meet di suppliers wey dey delay her goods.

questions.q: Read the sentence carefully and choose the option that best explains it: 'By the time the invigilator entered the examination hall, only two candidates had completed the objective questions.'
o: Exactly two candidates were absent from the examination.
Most candidates had not yet finished the objective questions when the invigilator came in.
The invigilator completed the objective questions for the candidates.
The invigilator entered late, after most candidates had already left.
questions.e: 'By the time' shows that one event had already happened before another. Since only two candidates had finished, it means the rest were still working when the invigilator entered.
questions.p: 'By the time' show say one thing don happen before another one. Na only two candidates don finish when invigilator enter, so the rest still dey work.

questions.q: Read the sentence carefully and choose the option that best explains it: 'The more carefully Aisha prepared her notes, the fewer mistakes she made in the test.'
o: Aisha made many mistakes despite preparing her notes carefully.
Aisha's carefulness in preparing notes had no effect on her test performance.
The fewer mistakes Aisha made, the more carefully she prepared her notes.
Careful preparation of notes led to a reduction in Aisha's mistakes.
questions.e: The 'the more... the fewer' structure shows a direct cause-and-effect link: as Aisha's care in preparing increased, her mistakes decreased.
questions.p: 'The more... the fewer' structure dey show say as Aisha dey careful well well for her notes, na so her mistakes dey reduce.

questions.q: Read the sentence carefully and choose the option that best explains it: 'Unless the local government fixes the bad road, traders will keep losing goods to accidents.'
o: The local government has already fixed the road, so losses will stop.
The traders will stop losing goods only if the bad road is repaired.
The bad road has nothing to do with the traders' losses.
Traders will lose goods only after the road has been fixed.
questions.e: 'Unless' introduces the only condition that can stop the stated problem. Here, repairing the road is the only thing that will end the traders' losses.
questions.p: 'Unless' na the only condition wey fit stop the problem. So na only if dem fix the road, traders go stop to dey lose their goods.

questions.q: Read the sentence carefully and choose the option that best explains it: 'Tunde's argument during the debate was like flogging a dead horse.'
o: Tunde was wasting his effort on a point that no longer mattered.
Tunde refused to take part in the debate.
Tunde physically harmed an animal during the debate.
Tunde presented a fresh and convincing new argument.
questions.e: 'Flogging a dead horse' is an idiom meaning to waste effort on something that is already settled or hopeless. It shows Tunde's point was pointless to keep pushing.
questions.p: 'Flogging dead horse' na idiom wey mean say person dey waste time for something wey don already finish or no get hope. E show say Tunde point no dey useful again.

questions.q: Read the sentence carefully and choose the option that best explains it: 'Hardly any of the students failed to submit their assignment before the deadline.'
o: Almost none of the students submitted their assignment before the deadline.
No student submitted the assignment before the deadline.
Almost all the students submitted their assignment before the deadline.
Only a few students submitted their assignment before the deadline.
questions.e: This sentence has a double negative: 'hardly any' plus 'failed to'. The two negatives cancel each other out, so the real meaning is that almost all the students succeeded in submitting on time.
questions.p: This sentence get double negative: 'hardly any' plus 'failed to'. The two negative dey cancel each other, so the real meaning be say almost everybody submit their work on time.

questions.q: Read the sentence carefully and choose the option that best explains it: 'Not a few of the candidates scored above average in the mock examination.'
o: Only a handful of candidates scored above average.
Exactly one candidate scored above average.
A large number of candidates scored above average.
questions.e: 'Not a few' is a figure of speech called litotes, which uses a negative to express a strong positive. It actually means 'many', so a large number of candidates scored above average.
questions.p: 'Not a few' na litotes, na figure of speech wey use negative talk to show strong positive meaning. E mean 'plenty', so na plenty candidates score above average.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. I am the class prefect this term, _____?
questions.e: The statement uses 'I am', so the tag must use 'I' with the opposite polarity. The correct short form is 'aren't I', which is the standard way English speakers form this tag. 'Am I' and 'are I not' are not grammatically acceptable tags.
questions.p: Since the sentence talk 'I am', the tag suppose be 'I' but turn the polarity. 'Aren't I' na the correct and common way to tag am. 'Am I' and 'are I not' no dey correct at all.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Musa injured _____ while playing football at the school field.
questions.e: The subject 'Musa' and the object refer to the same person, so a reflexive pronoun is needed. 'Himself' is the correct reflexive form for a singular male subject. 'Hisself' is not standard English, and 'him' or 'his' do not show the reflexive meaning.
questions.p: Musa na the same person wey do the action and still receive am, so we need reflexive pronoun. 'Himself' na the correct one for singular man. 'Hisself' no be correct English, and 'him' or 'his' no fit show say na himself he injure.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Let's finish this assignment before the test, _____?
questions.e: When a sentence begins with 'Let's' to suggest a joint action, the standard question tag is 'shall we', regardless of the main verb's tense. This is a fixed exception in English grammar. The other options do not follow this special rule for 'let's' sentences.
questions.p: When sentence start with 'Let's' to suggest say make we do something together, the correct tag na 'shall we', no matter the tense of the main verb. Na special grammar rule be dat for 'let's' sentences. The other options no follow dis special rule.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The teacher _____ class performed best in the quiz was transferred to another school.
questions.e: The gap requires a possessive relative pronoun because it shows ownership: the class belongs to the teacher. 'Whose' is used to show possession for people. 'Who' and 'whom' refer to people but do not show possession, and 'which' is used for things, not people.
questions.p: The gap need possessive relative pronoun because e dey show say the class na the teacher own. 'Whose' na the one wey dem dey use show possession for person. 'Who' and 'whom' na for person but dem no show possession, and 'which' na for things, no be person.

questions.q: Choose the option with the correct order of adjectives to complete the sentence: Mr. Adeyemi bought a ______ table for his new office in Lagos.
questions.e: In English, adjectives usually follow the order: opinion, size, material. 'Beautiful' is opinion, 'large' is size, and 'wooden' is material, so this order is correct.
questions.p: For English, adjective dey follow order: opinion, size, material. 'Beautiful' na opinion, 'large' na size, 'wooden' na material, so this order correct well well.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Ngozi ______ attends the morning assembly because she lives very far from the school.
questions.e: The adverb of frequency 'rarely' comes directly before the main verb 'attends' when there is no auxiliary verb present. 'Rarely attends' is the correct natural structure.
questions.p: When no auxiliary verb dey, adverb of frequency like 'rarely' go stand before the main verb. So 'rarely attends' na the correct way to arrange am.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: The baby slept ______ throughout the stormy night.
questions.e: The word that describes how the baby slept (a verb) must be an adverb. 'Peacefully' is the adverb form, while 'peaceful' is an adjective that cannot modify a verb.
questions.p: The word wey go describe how the baby sleep (verb) must be adverb. 'Peacefully' na the adverb, but 'peaceful' na adjective wey no fit modify verb.

questions.q: Choose the option with the correct order of adjectives to complete the sentence: The village chief owns a ______ hut.
questions.e: The usual adjective order is age, shape, then material. 'Old' shows age, 'round' shows shape, and 'mud' shows material, so 'old round mud' follows the correct sequence.
questions.p: The normal adjective order na age, shape, then material. 'Old' na age, 'round' na shape, 'mud' na material, so 'old round mud' follow the correct order.

questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the letters in CAPITALS: PEN
questions.e: The word 'PEN' has the vowel sound /e/ as in 'pen'. 'SAID' is pronounced /sed/, which has the same /e/ sound. The other words have different vowel sounds.
questions.p: 'PEN' get the /e/ sound. 'SAID' na /sed/, e get the same /e/ sound. The other words no match am.

questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the letters in CAPITALS: MOON
questions.e: 'MOON' has the long vowel sound /u:/. 'BLUE' is pronounced /blu:/, which carries the same /u:/ sound. 'BOOK' and 'GOOD' have the short /ʊ/ sound, while 'POT' has /ɒ/.
questions.p: 'MOON' get long /u:/ sound. 'BLUE' na /blu:/, e get the same /u:/ sound. 'BOOK' and 'GOOD' get short /ʊ/, 'POT' get /ɒ/.

questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the letters in CAPITALS: CHAIR
questions.e: 'CHAIR' has the diphthong sound /eə/. 'THERE' is pronounced /ðeə/, matching this sound. 'FEAR' and 'HEAR' have /ɪə/, while 'STAR' has /ɑ:/.
questions.p: 'CHAIR' get the /eə/ sound. 'THERE' na /ðeə/, e match am well well. 'FEAR' and 'HEAR' get /ɪə/, 'STAR' get /ɑ:/.

questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the letters in CAPITALS: BUS
questions.e: 'BUS' has the short vowel sound /ʌ/. 'LOVE' is pronounced /lʌv/, which has the same /ʌ/ sound. 'PUSH' has /ʊ/, 'BOSS' has /ɒ/, and 'PARK' has /ɑ:/.
questions.p: 'BUS' get short /ʌ/ sound. 'LOVE' na /lʌv/, e get the same /ʌ/. 'PUSH' get /ʊ/, 'BOSS' get /ɒ/, 'PARK' get /ɑ:/.

questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the letters in CAPITALS: FEAR
questions.e: 'FEAR' has the diphthong /ɪə/. 'HERE' is pronounced /hɪə/, matching this sound exactly. 'HAIR' has /eə/, 'HER' has /ɜ:/, and 'HEART' has /ɑ:/.
questions.p: 'FEAR' get /ɪə/ sound. 'HERE' na /hɪə/, e match am correct correct. 'HAIR' get /eə/, 'HER' get /ɜ:/, 'HEART' get /ɑ:/.

questions.q: Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: SHip
questions.e: The letters SH in 'ship' represent the sound /sh/. 'Chef' also has this /sh/ sound, borrowed from French spelling. 'Church' has /ch/, 'ghost' has /g/, and 'psalm' has /s/, so they do not match.
questions.p: Di SH for 'ship' na /sh/ sound. 'Chef' get di same /sh/ sound because of how dem borrow am from French. 'Church' na /ch/, 'ghost' na /g/, 'psalm' na /s/, so dem no match.

questions.q: Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: KNow
questions.e: In 'know', the K is silent, so KN represents the sound /n/. 'Gnaw' also has a silent G, leaving the /n/ sound. 'Keen' begins with /k/, 'ghost' begins with /g/, and 'psychology' begins with /s/, so none of these match /n/.
questions.p: For 'know', di K no dey sound, so KN be /n/ sound. 'Gnaw' also get silent G, so na /n/ remain. 'Keen' na /k/, 'ghost' na /g/, 'psychology' na /s/, so dem no match /n/.

questions.q: Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: WRite
questions.e: In 'write', the W is silent, so WR gives the sound /r/. 'Rhyme' also has a silent H, leaving the /r/ sound. 'Wet' begins with /w/, 'know' begins with /n/, and 'ghetto' begins with /g/, so they do not match /r/.
questions.p: For 'write', di W no dey sound, so WR na /r/ sound. 'Rhyme' also get silent H, so na /r/ remain. 'Wet' na /w/, 'know' na /n/, 'ghetto' na /g/, so dem no match /r/.

questions.q: Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: saVE
questions.e: The letters VE in 'save' represent the sound /v/, with the final E silent. 'Vow' also begins with the /v/ sound. 'Wine', 'when', and 'wet' all begin with /w/, which is a different sound from /v/, so they do not match.
questions.p: Di VE for 'save' na /v/ sound, di last E no dey sound. 'Vow' too start with /v/ sound. 'Wine', 'when', and 'wet' dey start with /w/, wey different from /v/, so dem no match.

questions.q: Study the words below. Each word is divided into syllables, and the stressed syllable is shown in CAPITAL letters. Choose the option in which the word is correctly stressed.
questions.e: Happy is a two-syllable word stressed on the first syllable: HAP-py. The other words are wrongly marked; garden, market and table are actually stressed on their first syllables too (GAR-den, MAR-ket, TA-ble), not as shown in options B, C and D.
questions.p: Happy na two-syllable word wey dem dey stress for the first part: HAP-py. The other words don show wrong stress; garden, market and table suppose stress for their first syllable (GAR-den, MAR-ket, TA-ble), no be like wetin dey options B, C and D.

questions.q: The word EXAMINATION is written below in four different stress patterns, with the stressed syllable in CAPITAL letters. Choose the option that shows the correct stress pattern.
questions.e: Examination has five syllables (ex-am-i-na-tion), and the stress falls on the fourth syllable: ex-am-i-NA-tion. Many words ending in '-tion' are stressed on the syllable just before the ending, as seen here.
questions.p: Examination get five syllables (ex-am-i-na-tion), and the stress dey fall for the fourth syllable: ex-am-i-NA-tion. Plenty words wey end with '-tion' dey stress the syllable before the ending, like wetin we see here.

questions.q: The word DEVELOPMENT is written below in four different stress patterns, with the stressed syllable in CAPITAL letters. Choose the option that shows the correct stress pattern.
questions.e: Development is stressed on the second syllable: de-VEL-op-ment. This is because its root word 'develop' is itself stressed on the middle syllable (de-VEL-op), and adding the suffix '-ment' does not change this stress.
questions.p: Development dey stress for the second syllable: de-VEL-op-ment. Na because the root word 'develop' dey stress for im middle syllable (de-VEL-op), and when dem add '-ment' e no change the stress.

questions.q: The word PHOTOGRAPHY is written below in four different stress patterns, with the stressed syllable in CAPITAL letters. Choose the option that shows the correct stress pattern.
questions.e: Photography is stressed on the second syllable: pho-TOG-ra-phy. This differs from the related word 'photograph' (PHO-to-graph), showing how adding the ending '-y' can shift the stress in a word family.
questions.p: Photography dey stress for the second syllable: pho-TOG-ra-phy. E different from 'photograph' (PHO-to-graph) — adding '-y' fit change where the stress dey sit for word family like this.

questions.q: The word ADVERTISEMENT is written below in four different stress patterns, with the stressed syllable in CAPITAL letters. In British English (the standard used by JAMB), choose the option that shows the correct stress pattern.
questions.e: In British English, 'advertisement' is stressed on the second syllable: ad-VER-tise-ment. This is a common exception that differs from how the shorter form 'advert' is stressed, so candidates must learn it specifically.
questions.p: For British English, 'advertisement' dey stress for the second syllable: ad-VER-tise-ment. Na one common exception wey different from how dem dey stress 'advert', so make students learn am well well.

questions.q:
In the sentence below, the word in capitals carries emphatic stress. Choose the question to which the sentence is the most appropriate answer.

Chidi gave his SISTER the textbook.
o: Who gave the textbook to Chidi's sister?
To whom did Chidi give the textbook?
Where did Chidi give the textbook?
What did Chidi give his sister?
questions.e: The stress is on SISTER, the person who received the textbook. So the sentence answers a question about who received it, that is, 'To whom did Chidi give the textbook?'
questions.p: Na SISTER dem put mouth for am, and she na the person wey receive the textbook. So the question wey fit am na 'To whom did Chidi give the textbook?'

questions.q:
In the sentence below, the word in capitals carries emphatic stress. Choose the question to which the sentence is the most appropriate answer.

Our teacher will travel to Kano NEXT WEEK.
o: When will our teacher travel to Kano?
Why will our teacher travel to Kano?
Where will our teacher travel to?
questions.e: NEXT WEEK tells us the time of the journey. The sentence therefore answers a question about when the teacher will travel, not where, who, or why.
questions.p: NEXT WEEK na the time wey dem go travel. So the sentence dey answer question about when the teacher go travel, no be where, who or why.

questions.q:
In the sentence below, the word in capitals carries emphatic stress. Choose the question to which the sentence is the most appropriate answer.

The farmer planted CASSAVA on his land.
o: Who planted cassava on his land?
When did the farmer plant cassava?
Where did the farmer plant cassava?
What did the farmer plant on his land?
questions.e: CASSAVA is the crop that was planted, so the stress highlights what was planted. The matching question must ask 'What did the farmer plant on his land?'
questions.p: CASSAVA na the thing wey the farmer plant, so the stress show what e plant. The question wey match am na 'What did the farmer plant on his land?'

questions.q:
In the sentence below, the word in capitals carries emphatic stress. Choose the question to which the sentence is the most appropriate answer.

Mr. Eze himself repaired the GENERATOR before the visitors arrived.
o: Why did Mr. Eze repair the generator?
When did Mr. Eze repair the generator?
What did Mr. Eze himself repair before the visitors arrived?
Who repaired the generator before the visitors arrived?
questions.e: Although 'himself' could suggest emphasis on the doer, the capitalised word here is GENERATOR, the object repaired. So the correct question must ask what was repaired, not who did it.
questions.p: Even though 'himself' fit make you think say na who dem dey emphasise, na GENERATOR dem capitalise, wey be the thing wey e fix. So the correct question na wetin dem fix, no be who fix am.

questions.q:
In the sentence below, the word in capitals carries emphatic stress. Choose the question to which the sentence is the most appropriate answer.

The headmaster, not the class teacher, gave Ngozi the AWARD.
o: Why did Ngozi receive the award?
What did the headmaster give Ngozi?
To whom did the headmaster give the award?
questions.e: Though the phrase 'not the class teacher' seems to stress the giver, the capitalised word is AWARD, the thing given. The sentence therefore answers 'What did the headmaster give Ngozi?'
questions.p: Even as 'not the class teacher' fit make you think say na the person wey give am dem dey emphasise, na AWARD dem capitalise, wey be the tin wey e give. So the question na 'What did the headmaster give Ngozi?'

questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: BREAK
questions.e: BREAK is pronounced /breɪk/. CAKE is pronounced /keɪk/, so both end with the same 'eɪk' sound. BEAK, BLACK and BRICK have different vowel sounds.
questions.p: BREAK dey sound as /breɪk/. CAKE too dey end with /eɪk/ sound, so dem match. BEAK, BLACK and BRICK no get that same sound.

questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: KNEE
questions.e: KNEE is pronounced /niː/, with a long 'ee' sound. SEA is pronounced /siː/, which has the same ending sound. NEW, NIGH and NET all have different vowel sounds.
questions.p: KNEE dey sound /niː/, with long 'ee'. SEA too get that same /iː/ sound for back. NEW, NIGH and NET no match am.

questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: COMB
questions.e: COMB is pronounced /koʊm/, with a silent 'b'. HOME is pronounced /hoʊm/, which matches this sound exactly. WOMB has a different vowel sound (/wuːm/), while COMMA and COMMON do not end in the same way.
questions.p: COMB dey sound /koʊm/, the 'b' no dey pronounce. HOME too be /hoʊm/, na the same sound be dat. WOMB get different vowel sound, and COMMA with COMMON no match am at all.

questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: SWORD
questions.e: SWORD is pronounced /sɔːrd/; the 'w' is silent. BOARD is also pronounced /bɔːrd/, giving the same ending sound. WORD, WORLD and SWARM all have different vowel sounds from SWORD.
questions.p: SWORD dey sound /sɔːrd/, the 'w' no dey pronounce. BOARD too be /bɔːrd/, so dem rhyme well well. WORD, WORLD and SWARM no get that same sound.

questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: YACHT
questions.e: YACHT is pronounced /jɒt/, not as its spelling suggests. ROT is also pronounced /rɒt/, which matches the ending sound exactly. CHAT, COAT and YACHTING have different vowel sounds.
questions.p: YACHT dey sound /jɒt/, e no follow as e spell. ROT too be /rɒt/, so the sound match well. CHAT, COAT and YACHTING get different vowel sound entirely.

questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: CHOIR
questions.e: CHOIR is pronounced /ˈkwaɪər/, ending in the same sound as FIRE, which is pronounced /ˈfaɪər/. CHORUS, QUIET and CHOP all have endings that sound nothing like this.
questions.p: CHOIR dey sound /ˈkwaɪər/, e dey end like FIRE wey be /ˈfaɪər/. CHORUS, QUIET and CHOP dia ending no resemble am at all.

questions.q: Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in quotes in the passive voice: "The headmaster will announce the results tomorrow."
o: The results will be announced by the headmaster tomorrow.
The results will announce by the headmaster tomorrow.
The results are been announced by the headmaster tomorrow.
The results were announced by the headmaster tomorrow.
questions.e: The original sentence is in the future simple active tense. To form the passive, we use 'will be' plus the past participle 'announced', keeping the future time reference 'tomorrow'.
questions.p: Di original sentence na future tense for active voice. To change am to passive, we go use 'will be' plus 'announced', and we still keep 'tomorrow' because di time no change.

questions.q: Choose the option that best expresses the same meaning as the sentence in quotes: "I am going to the market now," Tunde told his sister.
o: Tunde told his sister that he was going to the market now.
Tunde told his sister that he is going to the market now.
Tunde told his sister that he was going to the market then.
Tunde told his sister that he had gone to the market then.
questions.e: In reported speech, the present continuous tense 'am going' changes to the past continuous 'was going', and the time word 'now' changes to 'then' because the reporting happens later. Option C correctly makes both changes.
questions.p: For reported speech, 'am going' go change to 'was going', and 'now' go change to 'then' because di tori don pass when you dey report am. Option C do both change well well.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: If I _____ enough money, I would build a borehole for my village.
questions.e: This sentence expresses an unreal or unlikely present situation, which is a second conditional. Second conditionals use the simple past tense ('had') in the if-clause, with 'would' in the main clause.
questions.p: Dis sentence dey talk about situation wey no real now, na second conditional. Second conditional dey use simple past ('had') for di if-clause, and 'would' for di main clause.

questions.q: Choose the option that best expresses the same meaning as the sentence in quotes: "Will you come to my house tomorrow?" Ngozi asked Bisi.
o: Ngozi asked Bisi if she will come to her house tomorrow.
Ngozi asked Bisi if she would come to her house the following day.
Ngozi asked Bisi that she would come to her house the following day.
Ngozi asked Bisi if she would come to his house the following day.
questions.e: A reported yes/no question needs 'if' or 'whether', the modal 'will' changes to 'would', and the time word 'tomorrow' changes to 'the following day'. Since Ngozi is female, 'my house' becomes 'her house', making option B correct.
questions.p: Wen you dey report yes/no question, you go use 'if' or 'whether', 'will' go change to 'would', and 'tomorrow' go change to 'the following day'. Since na Ngozi (woman) talk am, 'my house' go turn 'her house', na why B correct.

questions.q: Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in quotes in the passive voice: "The committee should have completed the project before the end of the year."
o: The project was supposed to complete by the committee before the end of the year.
The project should be completed by the committee before the end of the year.
The project should have been completed by the committee before the end of the year.
The project should have completed by the committee before the end of the year.
questions.e: The active sentence uses a modal perfect structure, 'should have completed'. To form the correct passive, we keep the modal perfect form but add 'been' plus the past participle, giving 'should have been completed'.
questions.p: Di active sentence get modal perfect structure, 'should have completed'. To change am to correct passive, you go still keep di modal perfect but add 'been' plus past participle, so e go be 'should have been completed'.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Before Chidinma could withdraw a large sum of money, the bank teller asked her to fill a _____ form at the counter.
questions.e: A 'withdrawal form' is the correct banking term for the document a customer completes to take out cash from their account. The other options refer to different banking actions, not taking money out.
questions.p: Na 'withdrawal form' be the correct banking word when person wan collect im money from counter. The other words na for different banking matter, no be for taking money out.

questions.q:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.
In legal usage, a person who makes a sworn written statement to be used as evidence in court is correctly called a _____.
questions.e: A 'deponent' is someone who swears to and signs a written statement (deposition) for use as evidence. A plaintiff brings the case, a defendant answers it, and a litigant is simply a party in a lawsuit, so these do not fit the meaning.
questions.p: 'Deponent' na the person wey swear and sign statement wey dem go use as evidence for court. Plaintiff na the one wey bring case, defendant na the one wey dem accuse, litigant na just party for case, so these ones no fit the meaning.

questions.q:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.
In medical register, a drug that is specifically used to reduce a patient's fever is correctly described as _____.
questions.e: The prefix 'pyreto-' relates to fever, so an 'antipyretic' is a drug that lowers body temperature during fever, like paracetamol. Antiseptics prevent infection on skin, anticoagulants stop blood clotting, and antihistamines treat allergic reactions, so none of these reduce fever specifically.
questions.p: 'Pyreto' mean fever, so 'antipyretic' na medicine wey dey reduce body temperature when person get fever, like paracetamol. Antiseptic dey prevent infection for skin, anticoagulant dey stop blood from clotting, antihistamine dey treat allergy, none of them be for fever well well.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: When Mr. Danladi's cheque could not be paid because his account had no sufficient funds, bankers say the cheque _____.
questions.e: In banking language, a cheque that cannot be paid due to lack of funds is said to have 'bounced'. 'Cleared' means it was successfully paid, 'endorsed' means it was signed over to another person, and 'discounted' refers to selling a bill before its due date.
questions.p: For banking language, if cheque no fit pay because no money dey account, dem go say the cheque 'bounced'. 'Cleared' mean say dem don pay am well, 'endorsed' mean say dem sign am give another person, 'discounted' na when dem sell bill before e reach due date.

questions.q:
Choose the option that best completes the gap.
In court proceedings, the term SUBPOENA refers to a legal document that _____.
o: grants bail to an accused person
summons a witness to appear in court
records the final judgment of the court
dismisses a case for lack of evidence
questions.e: A 'subpoena' is a court order compelling a person to attend and give evidence or produce documents in a case. It is not about bail, dismissing a case, or recording judgment, which are different legal processes.
questions.p: 'Subpoena' na court order wey dey force person to come court give evidence or bring document. E no be about bail, dismissing case, or recording judgment, those ones na different legal matter.

questions.q: Choose the option OPPOSITE in meaning to the word in capitals: The landlord was very LENIENT with tenants who paid their rent late.
questions.e: LENIENT means mild or tolerant in dealing with people. The opposite is strict, which means firm and demanding in enforcing rules.
questions.p: Lenient mean say pesin soft-hearted or dey forgive well well when person do wrong. Di opposite na strict, wey mean say pesin tight-fisted and serious with rules.

questions.q: Choose the option OPPOSITE in meaning to the word in capitals: The chief's speech at the coronation was so AMBIGUOUS that the villagers argued over its true meaning.
questions.e: AMBIGUOUS means having more than one possible meaning, causing confusion. The opposite is clear, meaning easy to understand with no confusion.
questions.p: Ambiguous mean something wey get plenty meaning, wey dey confuse people. Di opposite na clear, wey mean say something plain and easy to understand.

questions.q: Choose the option OPPOSITE in meaning to the word in capitals: Although the twins looked alike, their characters were strikingly DIVERGENT.
questions.e: DIVERGENT means different or moving apart from each other. The opposite is similar, meaning alike or having common features.
questions.p: Divergent mean things wey dey different or dey go separate ways. Di opposite na similar, wey mean say dem resemble each other well well.

questions.q: Choose the option OPPOSITE in meaning to the word in capitals: The governor's VOLUBLE defence of the new policy surprised journalists who expected a short statement.
questions.e: VOLUBLE describes someone who talks a lot, fluently and at length. Its opposite, taciturn, describes a person who speaks very little.
questions.p: Voluble na person wey sabi talk plenty grammar up and down without tire. Di opposite na taciturn, wey be quiet pesin wey no like talk too much.

questions.q: Choose the option OPPOSITE in meaning to the word in capitals: Many customers found the trader's prices EXORBITANT compared to other shops in the market.
questions.e: EXORBITANT means unreasonably high, especially for a price. The opposite is reasonable, meaning fair and moderate.
questions.p: Exorbitant mean price wey too cost pass normal limit. Di opposite na reasonable, wey mean say price fair and fit person pocket.

questions.q: Choose the option OPPOSITE in meaning to the word in capitals: The soldiers were praised for remaining STEADFAST even when the enemy's attack intensified.
questions.e: STEADFAST means firm, loyal, and unshaken in purpose. The opposite is wavering, meaning unsteady or showing indecision.
questions.p: Steadfast mean pesin wey stand gidigba and no dey shake for wetin e believe. Di opposite na wavering, wey mean pesin mind dey shake up and down.

questions.q: Choose the option OPPOSITE in meaning to the word in capitals: Critics described the senator's argument as SPECIOUS once the facts were carefully examined, even though it had sounded convincing at first.
questions.e: SPECIOUS describes something that appears true or correct at first but is actually false or misleading. The opposite is genuine, meaning real and truthful.
questions.p: Specious mean something wey look like true at first glance but na lie. Di opposite na genuine, wey mean original and true thing.

questions.q: Choose the option OPPOSITE in meaning to the word in capitals: The accountant's report, though brief, was PERSPICUOUS enough for even non-experts in the boardroom to understand without further explanation.
questions.e: PERSPICUOUS means clearly expressed and easy to understand. Its opposite, obscure, means unclear or difficult to comprehend.
questions.p: Perspicuous mean matter wey clear like crystal and easy to grab. Di opposite na obscure, wey mean something dark and hard to understand.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Rather than face the shame of public disgrace, the former minister chose to ________ from his position.
questions.e: Resign specifically means to give up a position or office, which matches the context of leaving to avoid disgrace. Retire implies leaving after long service, not due to shame, so it does not fit as well.
questions.p: Resign mean say you comot for work sake of say you no want shame. Retire na when person don work finish before e comot, so resign correct pass.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The young lawyer presented her argument with such ________ that even the senior judges were impressed by her confidence and clarity.
questions.e: Aplomb means self-confidence and composure, which suits a lawyer who impresses judges with clarity. Arrogance has a negative tone that would not please the judges, so it is the wrong fit.
questions.p: Aplomb mean say you get confidence and you no dey shake. Since the lawyer impress the judges, na confidence she show, no be arrogance.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Although the twins were raised in the same house, their characters are completely ________; one is calm while the other is hot-tempered.
questions.e: Divergent means different or moving apart, which matches the contrast between calm and hot-tempered characters. Convergent means coming together, which contradicts the idea of difference expressed in the sentence.
questions.p: Divergent mean say things no be the same. Since one twin calm and the other one get hot temper, e show say their character no match.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The village elders tried to ________ the quarrel between the two families before it degenerated into a full-blown feud.
questions.e: Mediate means to intervene in a dispute to bring about an agreement, which fits the elders' peace-making role. Instigate, aggravate and provoke all mean to worsen or start trouble, the opposite of what the elders intended.
questions.p: Mediate mean say you want settle fight between two people. The elders want peace, so na mediate dem go do, no be to make the matter worse.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The newly appointed accountant was so ________ in handling the company's funds that not a single kobo was found missing after the audit.
questions.e: Scrupulous means extremely careful and honest about details, which explains why no money was missing after the audit. Frivolous and careless suggest a lack of seriousness, which would not lead to such an accurate result.
questions.p: Scrupulous mean say you dey very careful and you no dey thief money. Because no kobo miss, e show say the accountant do well well.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The professor's lecture was too ________ for the first-year students, who struggled to follow his complex theories and technical terms.
questions.e: Abstruse means difficult to understand, which matches the students struggling with complex theories. Lucid and elementary mean clear or simple, which would not cause the students to struggle as described.
questions.p: Abstruse mean say something hard to understand. If the students dey struggle with the lecture, e mean say the matter too deep for dem.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Having worked tirelessly for thirty years without complaint, Mrs. Adeyemi felt that a ________ retirement package was the least the company could offer her.
questions.e: Befitting means appropriate or suitable, which fits a reward that matches thirty years of dedicated service. Meagre, paltry and trivial all mean small or insignificant, which contradicts the idea of a deserved reward.
questions.p: Befitting mean say something correct and e fit the person. After thirty years of work, the woman deserve something wey fit her effort, no be small thing.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Measles, like many other childhood diseases, _______ common among unvaccinated children in some rural communities.
questions.e: Measles is the name of a disease and is treated as a singular uncountable noun. It therefore takes the singular verb is.
questions.p: Measles na disease name wey dem dey take as singular word, even though e dey ending with 's'. Na why e suppose carry singular verb like is.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The scissors Grandma gave to Chidinma for her tailoring class _______ already blunt.
questions.e: Scissors is a plural noun that always takes a plural verb, so are is correct. Words like scissors, trousers and glasses behave this way in English.
questions.p: Scissors na plural word wey must always carry plural verb like are. Words like trousers and glasses dey follow this same rule.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The quality of the mangoes sold at that roadside stall in Benin _______ improved greatly this season.
questions.e: The subject of the sentence is quality, a singular noun, not mangoes which is inside a prepositional phrase. A singular subject requires the singular verb has.
questions.p: Na quality be the true subject of this sentence, no be the mangoes. Since quality na singular, na has you go use.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Bread and butter _______ what Ngozi usually eats before going to school.
questions.e: Bread and butter refers to a single dish here, so it is treated as one idea taking a singular verb, is. If the items were separate foods, a plural verb would be used instead.
questions.p: Bread and butter for this sentence na one single food item. Na why e dey take singular verb like is.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Each of the new textbooks that the state government distributed to the schools _______ a unique serial number.
questions.e: Each is always singular regardless of the plural noun that follows it in the of-phrase. The correct singular verb form is has.
questions.p: Word like each dey always singular, even if plural noun come after am. Na why has be the correct verb to use.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The number of students from Enugu who _______ admitted into federal universities this year has risen sharply.
questions.e: The verb inside the relative clause who agrees with students, its plural antecedent, so were is required. Note that the main verb has risen later agrees instead with the singular subject number, showing the two clauses are judged separately.
questions.p: The verb inside the relative clause dey follow students, wey be plural word. Dat na why you must use were.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. By the end of this academic session, Ngozi _______ in this school for exactly six years.
questions.e: An action continuing up to a specific point in the future is expressed with the future perfect tense, will have taught. The phrase by the end of this session signals a completed duration at a future time.
questions.p: If you wan talk about something wey go don finish for future, you must use future perfect. Since the time never reach, 'will have taught' na the correct one.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Scarcely _______ the examination officer sealed the envelope when a loud knock startled everyone in the hall.
questions.e: The inverted structure 'Scarcely had...when' requires the past perfect auxiliary had. This shows one past action was completed just before another past action occurred.
questions.p: When you use 'Scarcely', you must follow am with 'had'. Na the correct way to show say one action happen before another one for past.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The watchman _______ the gate every night before the family returns from Lagos.
questions.e: A habitual action that happens regularly is expressed with the simple present tense, so locks is correct. The phrase every night confirms the habitual nature of the action.
questions.p: Because the man dey lock the gate every night, na simple present tense you go use. 'Locks' show say na wetin e dey do always.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. My uncle suggested that the contractor _______ the bad road before the rainy season begins.
questions.e: After verbs of suggestion like suggested, the subjunctive mood requires the base form of the verb regardless of the subject, so repair is correct. This is often called the mandative subjunctive.
questions.p: When you suggest something, the verb wey follow must be the base form. No matter who the person be, just use 'repair' as e be.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Look at those dark clouds gathering; it _______ heavily before we get home.
questions.e: A prediction about the near future based on present evidence is expressed with the simple future tense, so will rain is correct. The dark clouds serve as a sign leading to the prediction.
questions.p: If you see sign like dark cloud, you go use 'will rain' to talk wetin go happen. Na prediction based on wetin you dey see now.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. By the time Grandma Funke clocked eighty last year, she _______ in Ibadan for over five decades.
questions.e: An action completed before another past event needs the past perfect tense, so had lived is correct. Her living in Ibadan was completed before she clocked eighty, which is also in the past.
questions.p: Since the woman don clock eighty for past, you must use past perfect. 'Had lived' show say the action finish before the birthday reach.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Despite several warnings from the coach, the young footballer continued to show ___ before the match, doing unnecessary tricks with the ball.
questions.e: Show off means to display one's abilities in a boastful manner, which matches the footballer doing unnecessary tricks. Show up means to arrive, show out has no such idiomatic meaning here, and show in is not a recognised phrasal verb.
questions.p: Show off mean say person dey show-case im strength to pepper people, wey con match wetin the footballer dey do with ball. Na correct grammar be that.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The committee members arrived at the venue ___ different times, yet the meeting still started promptly at ten o'clock.
questions.e: The preposition at is used with specific points in time, such as ten o'clock, and also fits naturally with the phrase different times referring to varying clock moments. On is used for days and dates, while in is used for longer periods like months or years.
questions.p: We dey use the preposition at when we dey talk about specific time like different times. Other ones like on and in no fit join am for this place.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Having studied law for six years, Barrister Okonkwo is well versed ___ constitutional matters and often advises government agencies.
questions.e: The correct expression is versed in, meaning knowledgeable or skilled in a subject. The other prepositions do not collocate correctly with versed in standard English usage.
questions.p: Na standard English to talk say person be 'versed in' any subject. The remaining prepositions no dey follow versed well for grammar.

questions.q:
Read the passage and answer the question that follows.
During the long rainy season, Mr Bello's farm was flooded, and he had to call ___ his neighbours for help to move his yams to higher ground before they rotted. His neighbours, being generous people, did not hesitate to assist him, and by evening the yams were safely stored in his barn.
Choose the option that best completes the gap in the passage.
questions.e: Call on someone means to visit or appeal to them for assistance, which fits Mr Bello appealing to his neighbours for help. Call for means to require or demand something, which does not fit a person being asked directly. The other options do not form correct phrasal verb combinations with call in this sense.
questions.p: To call on person mean say you go meet them make dem help you. Na im make Mr Bello call on im neighbours for help.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The students were warned not to ___ their differences before the examination hall, as fighting would lead to immediate suspension.
questions.e: Fall out over means to quarrel about something, which matches students fighting over their differences. Fall back on means to rely on something as a last resort, and fall through means to fail to happen, so neither fits the context of quarrelling before an exam.
questions.p: Fall out over mean say people dey fight or quarrel because of something. Naim be say students no suppose fall out over their differences.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The market woman insisted that she would not sell the wrapper for less than one thousand naira, ___ how much the customer bargained.
questions.e: No matter how much is the correct idiomatic expression showing that the bargaining would not change her price. Regardless and irrespective should be followed by of, not to, and despite of is grammatically incorrect since despite does not take of.
questions.p: No matter how much na the correct way to talk am. Grammar no allow regardless to or despite of for this kind sentence.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The electrician warned the tenants that the faulty wiring could ___ a fire if it was not fixed immediately.
questions.e: Result in is the correct phrasal combination meaning to cause or lead to an outcome, here a fire. The other prepositions, of, with, and for, do not form standard collocations with result when describing a consequence.
questions.p: Result in mean say something go cause another thing to happen, like fire. Na only result in correct for this grammar.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The new intern was told to look ___ the filing system before attempting to reorganise it.
questions.e: Look into means to investigate or examine something carefully. The sentence requires the intern to study the system before changing it, which fits this meaning.
questions.p: Look into mean say make you check something well-well. Since the intern need to study the system before e change am, na the correct word be that.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Instead of confessing immediately, the suspect tried to talk his way ___ the accusation.
questions.e: Talk your way out of something means to use clever speech to avoid blame or trouble. The suspect was trying to escape the accusation by talking, so this phrase fits.
questions.p: Talk your way out of something mean say you dey use better talk take comot from trouble. The suspect dey try use talk escape the blame.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The governor's speech touched ___ several sensitive issues without going into full detail on any of them.
questions.e: Touch on means to mention a subject briefly. The sentence shows the governor mentioned issues without detailed discussion, which is the exact meaning of this phrasal verb.
questions.p: Touch on mean say you just mention something small-small. The governor talk about the matter but e no go deep inside.

questions.q: In the following sentence, identify the option that is used in the same way as the capitalised preposition. The teacher stood BY her promise to reward the best student in the class.
o: He arrived BY six o'clock as promised
The thief ran away BY the back door
She has always stood BY her husband through difficult times
The workers protested BY the gate of the factory
questions.e: In the given sentence, stood BY means remained loyal to or supported a commitment. Only the second option uses stood BY with this same meaning of supporting someone faithfully.
questions.p: Stood by for the sentence mean say you dey loyal to your promise. Na only the second option get that same meaning of support.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Because the two brothers could not see eye ___ eye on how to share their late father's land, the matter was taken to the family elders.
questions.e: See eye to eye is a fixed idiomatic expression meaning to agree with someone. The sentence describes disagreement between the brothers, so the correct preposition completing this idiom is required.
questions.p: See eye to eye na idiom wey mean say two people agree. Since the brothers no agree, na that preposition be the correct one for the idiom.

questions.q:
Read the passage and answer the question that follows. Tunde had always wanted to set up his own transport business in Ibadan. After saving diligently for three years, he finally gathered enough capital. However, just when he was about to purchase his first bus, the price of vehicles shot up due to a sudden rise in import duties. Tunde had to put off his plans and continue saving, hoping that prices would eventually come down. What does the phrase 'put off' mean as used in the passage?

Which option best explains why Tunde 'put off' his plans?
o: He postponed his plans to a later time
He discouraged others from starting the business
He changed his plans to a different business
He cancelled his business plans completely
questions.e: Put off means to delay or postpone something to another time. The passage shows Tunde still intends to buy the bus later once prices improve, showing postponement rather than cancellation.
questions.p: Put off mean say you shift something to another time. Tunde no cancel him plan, e just wait make price come down first.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the expression in quotes. When the examination results were released, Tope discovered that her best friend had 'played to the gallery' during the debate competition.
o: Won the competition through honest effort
Refused to participate in the competition at all
Performed insincerely to impress the audience rather than to express true conviction
questions.e: To 'play to the gallery' means to act or speak in a way designed to appeal to onlookers rather than out of genuine belief. It does not mean refusing to take part or preparing well.
questions.p: To 'play to the gallery' mean say person dey act abi talk just to sweet mouth people make dem clap for am, instead make e talk wetin dey him heart. E no mean say person refuse to join competition abi say e read well.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the expression in quotes. Because the landlord kept increasing the rent without any improvement to the building, the tenants decided it was time to 'put their foot down'.
o: Report the matter to the police
Move out of the building immediately
Walk away quietly from the argument
Firmly refuse to accept the situation any longer
questions.e: 'Put one's foot down' means to take a firm stand and insist on something, usually to stop an unwanted situation. It does not specifically mean moving out or reporting to the police.
questions.p: To 'put your foot down' mean say you don stand gidigba say you no gree for nonsense again, especially when you wan stop bad tin. E no mean say you pack commot for house abi report mata to police.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the expression in quotes. Mr. Adeyemi, the school principal, warned the teachers to 'toe the line' or face disciplinary action during the inspection week.
o: Compete against one another for recognition
Walk carefully along a marked path
Conform strictly to the accepted rules and standards
Stand in a straight queue for the inspectors
questions.e: 'Toe the line' means to comply with rules or expected standards of behaviour. It has nothing to do with physically standing in a queue or walking along a path.
questions.p: To 'toe the line' mean say you must follow all the rules and regulations wey dem give you. E no get anything to do with to stand for straight line abi to dey waka for road.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the expression in quotes. Despite losing his job suddenly, Emeka refused to 'throw in the towel' and kept searching for new opportunities.
questions.e: 'Throw in the towel' is a boxing-derived idiom meaning to give up or surrender in the face of difficulty. Emeka's continued search shows he did not give up.
questions.p: To 'throw in the towel' na boxing language wey mean say person don give up or surrender because trouble don too much. Emeka's action show say e no give up at all.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the expression in quotes. The young lawyer's brilliant defence of the accused market woman left the senior judges 'eating their words'.
o: Withdrawing or regretting what they had earlier said
Praising the lawyer openly in public
Feeling hungry after the long court session
Agreeing to retire from their positions
questions.e: To 'eat one's words' means to retract a previous statement, usually because it has been proven wrong. The judges must have earlier doubted the young lawyer, so his success forced them to withdraw their opinion.
questions.p: To 'eat one's words' mean say person must take back wetin e talk before because e don see say e talk wrong. The judges must don talk down the lawyer before, naim make the lawyer brilliance scatter their mouth.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the expression in quotes. The governor's aide was accused of being a 'turncoat' after he abandoned his party just before the election.
o: Someone who changes loyalty or allegiance for personal gain
Someone who always tells the truth
Someone who speaks two languages fluently
Someone who dresses in expensive clothes
questions.e: A 'turncoat' is a person who deserts one group, cause, or party to join an opposing one, often for selfish reasons. This matches the aide abandoning his party before the election.
questions.p: A 'turncoat' na person wey dey run leave him party abi group go join another one because of wetin e wan gain. E fit well with how the aide leave him party before election.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the expression in quotes. After the court dismissed the case against him for lack of evidence, the businessman was said to have 'got off scot-free'.
o: Paid a heavy fine to settle the matter
Escaped punishment completely despite being guilty or suspected
Was sentenced to a short prison term
questions.e: 'Get off scot-free' means to avoid punishment or blame entirely, often when one might have deserved some consequence. The dismissal of the case allowed him to escape without any penalty.
questions.p: To 'get off scot-free' mean say person escape punishment or trouble completely. Since court throw away the case, the businessman waka go free without any penalty.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the expression in quotes. Ngozi's father told her that marrying a man she barely knew was like 'buying a pig in a poke'.
o: Making a wise investment after careful thought
Trusting a close family friend completely
Getting something without first checking its true quality or worth
Purchasing farm animals at a cheap price
questions.e: 'Buy a pig in a poke' means to acquire or agree to something without first examining or verifying it, which carries great risk. Her father is warning that marrying someone unknown is a similar blind risk.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the sentence: 'Only when the results were released did Ngozi realise she had actually passed the examination.'
o: Ngozi never found out whether she passed or not
Ngozi doubted the results even after they were released
Ngozi realised she had passed before the results were released
Ngozi did not know she had passed until the results came out
questions.e: The inverted structure 'only when...did' means the realisation happened solely at that point, not earlier. So Ngozi discovered she had passed only after the results were out.
questions.p: That grammar 'only when...did' mean say na that time wey result come out she come know say she pass. E show clearly say she no sabi before until result show.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the sentence: 'Segun's excuse for missing the meeting was as thin as it was unconvincing.'
o: Segun's excuse convinced everyone at the meeting
Segun did not give any excuse at all
Segun gave a very weak and unbelievable excuse
Segun's excuse was short but believable
questions.e: Describing an excuse as 'thin' means it lacks substance, and pairing it with 'unconvincing' reinforces that it failed to persuade anyone. Both words point to a weak, implausible excuse.
questions.p: To say excuse 'thin' and 'unconvincing' mean say the reason wey person give no get head at all. Na very weak lie wey nobody go fit believe.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the sentence: 'It is not that Fatima cannot speak French; rather, she simply chooses not to in public.'
o: Fatima speaks French only when forced to
Fatima can speak French but deliberately avoids doing so publicly
Fatima is unable to speak French at all
Fatima is learning French but has not mastered it
questions.e: The construction 'not that...rather' corrects a wrong assumption about ability and replaces it with the real reason, which is personal choice. So Fatima has the skill but avoids using it openly.
questions.p: E mean say Fatima sabi speak French well well, na just her choice say she no like to dey speak am for open place. She get the skill, but she dey keep am.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the sentence: 'Had the contractor followed the approved building plan, the bridge at Yenagoa would not have collapsed during the flood.'
o: The contractor did not follow the plan, and the bridge collapsed
The bridge would have collapsed regardless of the plan used
The bridge collapsed even though there was no flood
The contractor followed the plan, yet the bridge still collapsed
questions.e: This is a third conditional expressing an unreal past condition, meaning the opposite actually happened. Since the plan was not followed, the bridge did in fact collapse during the flood.
questions.p: Dis na past conditional wey show say because the contractor no follow plan, the bridge come fall down. Ifim follow am, bridge for no fall during that flood.

questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the sentence: 'Were it not for the timely intervention of the neighbours, the fire at the Okafors' warehouse would have destroyed the entire street.'
o: The fire destroyed the entire street despite the neighbours' help
The neighbours arrived too late to make any difference
The neighbours caused the fire to spread further
The neighbours' help prevented the fire from destroying the whole street
questions.e: This subjunctive conditional shows that without the neighbours' action, a worse outcome would have occurred. Since they did intervene in time, the wider destruction was actually averted.
questions.p: E mean say if not for as neighbors quick come help quench fire, everywhere for don scatter. Na their quick action save the whole street from burning down.

questions.q: Read the sentence carefully and choose the option that best explains it: 'So thorough was the auditor's investigation that not a single discrepancy in the company's accounts escaped his notice.'
o: The auditor overlooked several discrepancies in the accounts
The company's accounts had no discrepancies to find
The auditor noticed every discrepancy because his investigation was very detailed
The auditor's investigation was careless and incomplete
questions.e: The inverted emphatic structure 'so thorough...that' stresses the high degree of care taken, leading to the result that nothing was missed. This means every discrepancy was detected due to the detailed investigation.
questions.p: That sentence dey explain say auditor work tight well well. Because im check everything clean-clean, im see all the mistake for inside the company account.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. This farmland belongs to my uncle and _____, not to the village council.
questions.e: After the preposition to, an object pronoun is needed, so me is correct. I is a subject pronoun and cannot follow to. Myself and mine are not suitable objects of a preposition here.
questions.p: Na 'me' suppose follow dis preposition 'to', no be 'I'. 'Myself' and 'mine' no fit follow dat 'to' for dis sentence.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The new minibus, _____ was donated by the old students' association, will convey the debate team to Enugu.
questions.e: Since the clause gives extra, non-essential information about the minibus (an object, not a person), it must be set off by commas and introduced by 'which'. 'That' cannot normally follow a comma in such a non-restrictive clause, and 'who/whom' are used for people only.
questions.p: Because we dey talk about minibus, we must use 'which' to join the sentence. We no fit use 'that' when comma dey there. 'Who' and 'whom' na for human being, so dem no fit work here.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. You will submit your project work on time, _____?
questions.e: The main statement is affirmative ('You will submit'), so the question tag must be negative, giving 'won't you'. 'Will you' is wrongly affirmative, while 'don't you' and 'shall you' do not match the modal verb 'will' used in the statement.
questions.p: If the main sentence na positive, the question tag must be negative. Since the sentence talk say 'You will', the tag must be 'won't you'. Other options no match the modal verb wey dey the sentence.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. Neither Adaeze nor her brothers have finished _____ project on renewable energy.
questions.e: With 'neither...nor' joining a singular and a plural noun, the pronoun should agree with the noun nearer to it, which here is 'brothers' (plural), so 'their' is correct. The other options wrongly agree with the singular 'Adaeze' or do not fit a group of people at all.
questions.p: When you use 'neither...nor', the pronoun must follow the noun wey near am. Since 'brothers' na plural, we must use 'their'. 'Her' or 'his' no go correct because dem be singular.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. The matter is strictly between you and _____, so do not discuss it with anyone else.
questions.e: Because the pronoun follows the preposition 'between' and works together with 'you' as objects, the objective case 'me' is required. 'I' is subjective, 'myself' is reflexive and unnecessary here, and 'mine' is possessive, none of which fit after a preposition in this way.
questions.p: After preposition like 'between', you must use object pronoun. 'Me' na the correct one to use here. 'I' na subject, so e no fit follow preposition.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap. It was Fatima and not her cousins _____ broke the vase in the staff room.
questions.e: The clause needs a subject pronoun referring to a person performing the action of breaking the vase, and since the emphasis is on Fatima as the one who did it, 'who' correctly serves as the subject of the relative clause. 'Whom' is an object form, 'which' refers to things, and 'whose' shows possession, none of which fit the subject role required here.
questions.p: We dey talk about person wey break the vase, so we must use 'who'. 'Whom' na for object, and 'which' na for thing. 'Who' na the correct subject pronoun for Fatima.

questions.q: Choose the option with the correct order of adjectives to complete the sentence: Grandma Osei kept a ______ basket in her store at Onitsha market.
questions.e: The normal English order of adjectives is size before age before shape before material. So small comes before old, which comes before round, which comes before wicker.
questions.p: Na correct English order of adjectives be size, age, shape, then material. Dem arrange am as small, old, round, and wicker.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Of the two routes to Ibadan, the express road is ______ one to take during the rainy season.
questions.e: When comparing exactly two things, the comparative form with 'the' is used, not the superlative. Since only two routes are being compared, 'the safer' is correct.
questions.p: If you dey compare just two things, na comparative form plus 'the' you go use. Na 'the safer' correct because na two routes dem dey talk.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Although the twins look alike, Kemi behaves ______ than her sister.
questions.e: The word modifies the verb 'behaves', so an adverb is needed, not an adjective. The comparative adverb form 'more responsibly' correctly compares the behaviour of the two sisters.
questions.p: Na adverb you need here to qualify the verb 'behaves', no be adjective. Na 'more responsibly' show how the two sisters take dey behave.

questions.q: In the sentence below, identify the part that shows the correct position of the adverb: 'Only the headmaster can approve that request.' Which word does the adverb 'only' modify?
questions.e: The adverb 'only' is placed right before 'the headmaster', showing that it limits or focuses on that noun phrase alone. Moving 'only' elsewhere in the sentence would change its meaning.
questions.p: Na 'the headmaster' the word 'only' dey qualify for that sentence. E mean say na only that person get power to approve am.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: The new intern at the hospital in Enugu is ______ to handle emergency cases without supervision.
questions.e: The adverb 'enough' always comes after the adjective it modifies, so the correct form is 'young enough'. This shows the intern lacks sufficient age or experience for the task.
questions.p: The word 'enough' suppose always follow the adjective wey e dey qualify. Na 'young enough' be the correct grammar for that place.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Because the market woman shouted ______, the thief ran away immediately.
questions.e: The word describes how the woman shouted, so an adverb is required rather than an adjective. 'Loudly' correctly modifies the verb 'shouted'.
questions.p: Na adverb wey be 'loudly' you go use to describe how she take shout. Adjective like 'loud' no fit qualify verb.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: ______ had the referee blown the final whistle than the fans stormed the pitch in Lagos.
questions.e: The structure 'no sooner...than' is a fixed inversion pattern used to show that one event happened immediately after another. The other words pair with 'when' instead of 'than'.
questions.p: Na 'No sooner' dey follow 'than' make sentence correct. The rest options like hardly or scarcely suppose use 'when'.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Adaeze speaks French ______ than her elder sister, who studied the language for only one year.
questions.e: An adverb is needed to modify the verb 'speaks', and since two people are being compared, the comparative form is required. More fluently correctly combines both requirements.
questions.p: Na adverb wey go qualify di verb 'speaks' we need here. Dem dey compare two people, so comparative form 'more fluently' correct well well.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: It was ______ hot that the farmers decided to rest under the mango tree until evening.
questions.e: The structure 'so + adjective + that' is used to show result or consequence. 'Such' would require a noun, as in 'such hot weather', so it does not fit here.
questions.p: Di pattern 'so + adjective + that' naim we dey use to show result. If na 'such', e suppose carry noun join am, so na 'so' fit this place.

questions.q: In the sentence: 'The restless children, who had waited patiently for hours, finally saw their father arrive,' identify the adverb and the word it modifies.
questions.e: Patiently is an adverb describing how the children waited, so it modifies the verb waited. Restless is an adjective describing children, and finally modifies the verb saw, not father.
questions.p: Word like patiently na adverb wey dey tell us how dem wait, so na di verb waited e dey qualify. Di other options no match at all.

questions.q: Choose the option with the correct order of adjectives to complete the sentence: The tailor sewed a ______ gown for the bride's wedding ceremony.
questions.e: The standard order of adjectives is opinion, size, colour, then material: beautiful (opinion), long (size), white (colour), silk (material). This order sounds natural to native and competent speakers of English.
questions.p: Correct order of adjective na opinion, size, colour, then material. Naim make 'beautiful long white silk' correct for dis sentence.

questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: ______ had the market women set up their stalls than the rain began to pour heavily.
questions.e: The fixed structure 'no sooner...than' is used to show that one action happened immediately after another. Hardly and scarcely require 'when' instead of 'than', making them incorrect here.
questions.p: Na 'no sooner' dey follow 'than' for dis kind sentence. Hard or scarcely suppose carry 'when', so na 'no sooner' correct.

questions.q: Choose the option in which all the words are correctly spelt.
questions.e: Accommodate, embarrass and occurrence all take double consonants in the correct spots. The other options drop one of the needed double letters.
questions.p: All those words get double letters for inside. If you no put them well, you go get the spelling wrong.

questions.q: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.
o: Mrs. Adeyemi our class teacher is traveling, to Kano tomorrow.
Mrs. Adeyemi, our class teacher, is traveling to Kano tomorrow.
Mrs. Adeyemi, our class teacher is traveling to Kano tomorrow.
Mrs. Adeyemi our class teacher, is traveling to Kano tomorrow.
questions.e: The phrase 'our class teacher' is an appositive explaining who Mrs. Adeyemi is, so it must be enclosed by a comma on both sides. The other options leave out one comma, breaking the pair.
